sections.title: Sounds and spelling
sections.summary: Italian spelling is very regular: once you know how c and g change before e and i, how double consonants are held, and where the stress falls, you can read almost any word aloud correctly. This chapter also covers the three special clusters gli, gn and sc.

rules.title: Five pure vowels, every one pronounced
rules.body: Italian has five vowel letters, a e i o u, and each is a short, clear sound: a as in 'father', e as in 'bed', i as in 'machine', o as in 'for', u as in 'rule'. Vowels are never reduced to a mumbled 'uh' and never silent, so a final -e or -o is always said: cane is CA-ne, not 'cane' as in English. Two vowels next to each other are both pronounced: paese is pa-E-se, aiuto is a-IU-to.

examples.en: dog (CA-ne, the final e is pronounced)

rules.title: c and g are soft before e and i, hard elsewhere
rules.body: Before e or i, c sounds like the ch of 'church' and g like the j of 'jam': cena (CHE-na), cinema, gelato, gita. Before a, o, u or a consonant they are hard, like k and the g of 'go': casa, cosa, cura, grande, gola. To keep the hard sound before e or i, Italian inserts an h: che, chi, ghe, ghi are pronounced ke, ki, ge, gi (hard). So chiesa is KIE-sa and spaghetti is spa-GET-ti.

rules.title: The softening i in cia, gio, giu
rules.body: To get the soft ch or j sound before a, o or u, Italian writes an i after the c or g: ciao, giorno, Giulia, arancia. In these spellings the i is usually not a separate vowel; it only marks the soft sound. So ciao is CHA-o (two syllables, not three), giorno is JOR-no and Giuseppe is ju-SEP-pe. Only when the i is stressed is it heard as a full vowel: farmacia is far-ma-CHI-a, and bugia (lie) is bu-JI-a.

rules.title: Double consonants are held longer and change meaning
rules.body: A written double consonant is pronounced noticeably longer than a single one, and the vowel before it is a little shorter. This is not decoration: many pairs of words differ only in this way. pala (shovel) vs palla (ball), nono (ninth) vs nonno (grandfather), sete (thirst) vs sette (seven), caro (dear) vs carro (cart), pena (pain) vs penna (pen). Practise holding the consonant: sette is SET-te, with a pause on the t.

rules.title: gli, gn and sc
rules.body: Three clusters have sounds English spells differently. gli sounds like the lli of 'million' with no g: famiglia, figlio, gli (the), aglio. gn sounds like the ny of 'canyon': gnocchi, bagno, signora, ogni. sc before e or i sounds like sh: pesce, scienza, uscire, sciare; before a, o, u or h it is sk: scuola, scarpa, schiena, scherzo. A few words keep gl as two sounds, mainly before i in glicine and negligente, but these are rare.

rules.title: Stress usually falls on the second-to-last syllable
rules.body: Most Italian words are stressed on the penultimate syllable: aMIco, raGAZza, itaLIAno, parLAre. A sizeable group is stressed on the third-from-last syllable with no written sign, so these must be learned: TAvola, teLEfono, MEdico, SAbato, ZUcchero. When stress falls on the final vowel it is always written with an accent: città, caffè, perché, università, lunedì. The accent is part of the spelling and cannot be dropped.

rules.title: Grave and acute accents, and the words they distinguish
rules.body: The grave accent (à è ì ò ù) is the normal one; the acute (é) appears only on a closed final e, as in perché, poiché, né and the number endings ventitré, trentatré. Accents also tell apart short words that would otherwise look the same: è (is) vs e (and), sì (yes) vs si (oneself), là (there) vs la (the), dà (gives) vs da (from), né (nor) vs ne (of it). On capital letters the accent is kept: È vero.

examples.en: Why? (acute accent on a closed e)

rules.title: h, r, s and z
rules.body: The letter h is always silent. It appears in four forms of avere (ho, hai, ha, hanno) to distinguish them from o, ai, a, anno, and after c and g to keep them hard. r is rolled with the tip of the tongue, and double rr is rolled longer: Roma, carro. s is voiced like English z between vowels (casa, rosa) and before voiced consonants (sbaglio), otherwise like s in 'sun'. z stands for two sounds, ts as in pizza, grazie, zio and dz as in zero, zaino, mezzo; the spelling does not show which, so learn each word.

examples.en: I have, you have, he/she has, they have (silent h)

exercises.q: How is the c pronounced in 'cena' (dinner)?
exercises.explain: c before e or i is soft, the ch sound: CHE-na.

exercises.q: Which word has a hard g, as in English 'go'?
exercises.explain: The h in ghiaccio keeps the g hard before i; the other three have soft g before e or i.

exercises.q: In Italian every vowel is pronounced, including a final -e.
exercises.explain: There are no silent vowels: cane is CA-ne, notte is NOT-te.
To keep c hard before i, Italian writes ch: chi.
sette with a long tt is seven; sete is thirst, seta is silk, setta is sect.

exercises.q: Double consonants are pronounced exactly like single consonants; the spelling is just a convention.
exercises.explain: Doubles are held longer and distinguish words: pala/palla, nono/nonno.

options: like n only, the g is silent
exercises.explain: gn is one sound, the ny of canyon: NYOK-ki.

options: like a hard g plus li
exercises.explain: gli is the ly sound of million; there is no g sound at all.

exercises.q: Complete the word for 'fish', which has the sh sound before e: pe___e
exercises.explain: sc before e or i is pronounced sh: pesce.
Before a, o or u, sc is sk; it is sh only before e and i.

exercises.q: Most Italian words are stressed on the second-to-last syllable.
exercises.explain: Penultimate stress is the default: aMIco, raGAZza, parLAre.

exercises.q: Which word is stressed on its final syllable?
exercises.explain: Final stress is always written with an accent: cit-TA.
caffè is stressed on the last syllable, so it carries a grave accent.

exercises.q: How is the h pronounced in 'ho' (I have)?
exercises.explain: h is always silent in Italian; in ho it only distinguishes the verb from o (or).

exercises.q: In 'ciao', the i is pronounced as a separate vowel: chee-AH-oh.
exercises.explain: The i only softens the c: ciao is CHA-o, two syllables.

exercises.q: Which word is pronounced with a k sound?
exercises.explain: ch before i is hard: KIE-sa; the others have soft c before i or e.
nonno has a long nn; nono is ninth, nano is dwarf, nove is nine.

exercises.q: 'io pago' is PA-go with a hard g. Write 'you pay' (tu), keeping the hard g before i: ___
exercises.explain: An h is inserted so that g stays hard before i: paghi.

exercises.q: 'perché' is written with an acute accent because its final e is a closed e.
exercises.explain: The acute accent marks a closed final e, as in perché and ventitré.

exercises.q: In 'zucchero' (sugar), what do the letters cch stand for?
exercises.explain: cch before e is a doubled hard k: ZUK-ke-ro.

exercises.q: Complete 'family' with the cluster that gives the ly sound: fami___a
exercises.explain: gli spells the ly sound of million: famiglia.

exercises.q: The z in 'pizza' is pronounced ts, as in 'cats'.
exercises.explain: pizza, grazie and zio have the voiceless ts; zero and zaino have dz.

sections.title: Nouns, gender and plurals
sections.summary: Every Italian noun is masculine or feminine, and its final vowel usually tells you which. The plural is formed by changing that final vowel, with a few spelling adjustments and a small set of irregular nouns worth learning early.

rules.title: -o is usually masculine, -a usually feminine
rules.body: Nouns ending in -o are almost all masculine (libro, ragazzo, tavolo, gatto) and nouns ending in -a are almost all feminine (casa, ragazza, pizza, scuola). Gender matters because articles, adjectives and past participles must agree with it. Exceptions exist but are few: la mano (hand), la foto, la moto, la radio and l'auto are feminine despite -o, mostly because they are shortenings of longer feminine words (fotografia, motocicletta, automobile).

rules.title: Nouns in -e can be either gender
rules.body: Nouns ending in -e must be learned with their gender: il cane (dog), il fiore (flower), il nome (name) are masculine; la notte (night), la chiave (key), la carne (meat) are feminine. Some endings are reliable guides: -zione and -sione are feminine (la stazione, la televisione), -tà and -tù are feminine (la città, la gioventù), -ore is masculine (il colore, il dottore), -ale and -ile are usually masculine (il giornale, il cortile).

rules.title: Regular plurals: -o to -i, -a to -e, -e to -i
rules.body: The plural changes the final vowel. Masculine -o becomes -i: libro, libri; ragazzo, ragazzi. Feminine -a becomes -e: casa, case; ragazza, ragazze. Nouns in -e become -i whatever their gender: cane, cani; notte, notti; stazione, stazioni. Italian never adds an s for the plural.

rules.title: Spelling changes with -co, -go, -ca, -ga, -cia, -gia
rules.body: Feminine -ca and -ga always keep the hard sound with an h: amica, amiche; riga, righe. Masculine -co and -go usually add h when the stress is on the syllable before the ending (albergo, alberghi; fuoco, fuochi; lago, laghi) but not when stress is earlier (medico, medici; psicologo, psicologi); the common word amico is an exception and gives amici (hard k is lost). For -cia and -gia: keep the i if it is stressed or follows a vowel (farmacia, farmacie; camicia, camicie; valigia, valigie), drop it after a consonant (arancia, arance; spiaggia, spiagge).

examples.en: friend, friends (exception: soft c in the plural)
orange, oranges (i dropped after a consonant)

rules.title: Nouns that do not change in the plural
rules.body: Several groups keep the same form in singular and plural, and only the article shows the number. Nouns with a final stressed vowel: la città, le città; il caffè, i caffè. Nouns ending in a consonant, mostly loanwords: il film, i film; lo sport, gli sport; il bar, i bar. Shortened nouns: la foto, le foto; l'auto, le auto; il cinema, i cinema. One-syllable nouns: il re, i re. Nouns ending in -i: la crisi, le crisi.

rules.title: Irregular plurals
rules.body: A few very common nouns have plurals to memorise. uomo becomes uomini (man, men). mano (feminine) becomes mani. A group of masculine nouns, mostly body parts and pairs, switch to a feminine plural in -a: l'uovo, le uova (egg); il braccio, le braccia (arm); il dito, le dita (finger); il ginocchio, le ginocchia (knee); il paio, le paia (pair); il centinaio, le centinaia (hundred). dio (god) becomes dei, and bue (ox) becomes buoi.

examples.en: the egg, the eggs (masculine singular, feminine plural)

rules.title: Masculine nouns in -a and nouns in -ista
rules.body: A set of nouns of Greek origin end in -a but are masculine and take the plural -i: il problema, i problemi; il programma, i programmi; il sistema, i sistemi; il tema, i temi; il clima, i climi; il poeta, i poeti. Nouns in -ista (jobs and followers) are the same for both genders in the singular and only the article shows the gender: il turista, la turista; il dentista, la dentista. In the plural they split: i turisti (masculine) but le turiste (feminine).

examples.en: the male tourist, the female tourist
the tourists (masculine or mixed), the tourists (all women)

rules.title: Nouns for people: pairs of forms
rules.body: Many nouns for people have a masculine and a feminine form. -o pairs with -a: amico, amica; ragazzo, ragazza; cuoco, cuoca. Some -e nouns add -essa for the feminine: studente, studentessa; professore, professoressa; dottore, dottoressa. -tore pairs with -trice: attore, attrice; scrittore, scrittrice; pittore, pittrice. Many -e and -ista nouns do not change: il cantante, la cantante; il giornalista, la giornalista. The masculine plural is used for a mixed group: i miei amici can include women; gli studenti means the students of both sexes.

examples.en: the male student, the female student
two friends (two men, or a man and a woman)

exercises.explain: Nouns ending in -o are almost always masculine: il libro.
Feminine -a becomes -e in the plural: casa, case.
Masculine -o becomes -i: ragazzo, ragazzi.

exercises.q: Nouns ending in -e are always feminine.
exercises.explain: -e nouns can be either gender: il cane, il fiore are masculine; la notte, la chiave are feminine.
Nouns in -e take -i in the plural, whatever their gender: cane, cani.
-e becomes -i: stazione, stazioni.

exercises.q: Which of these nouns is feminine?
exercises.explain: Nouns in -tà are feminine (la città); problema, fiore and giornale are all masculine.

exercises.q: 'città' has the same form in the singular and the plural.
exercises.explain: Nouns with a final stressed vowel do not change: la città, le città.
amico is an exception: no h is added, so the plural amici has a soft c.

exercises.q: What is the plural of 'amica' (female friend)?
exercises.explain: Feminine -ca always becomes -che to keep the hard k: amica, amiche.
-go with stress on the previous syllable adds h: albergo, alberghi.
uomo has the irregular plural uomini.

exercises.q: 'mano' (hand) is masculine because it ends in -o.
exercises.explain: mano is one of the few feminine -o nouns: la mano, le mani.
Masculine nouns in -a of Greek origin take the plural -i: problemi.

exercises.q: Which noun ends in -a but is masculine?
exercises.explain: programma, like problema and sistema, is masculine: il programma, i programmi.
-tore pairs with -trice: attore, attrice.
professore adds -essa for the feminine: professoressa.

exercises.q: 'il cantante' and 'la cantante' are both correct: the noun itself does not change.
exercises.explain: Many -e nouns for people are the same for both sexes; only the article shows the gender.
foto is short for fotografia and does not change: la foto, le foto.
After a consonant the i of -cia is dropped: arancia, arance.
The i is stressed in farmacia, so it is kept: farmacie.

options: two male friends or a man and a woman
exercises.explain: The masculine plural covers all-male and mixed groups; two women would be due amiche.

exercises.answer: Ho due fratelli e una sorella.
exercises.en: I have two brothers and one sister.

exercises.q: 'dita' is the plural of 'dito' (finger) and is feminine.
exercises.explain: dito belongs to the group with a feminine plural in -a: il dito, le dita.
Nouns ending in a consonant do not change in the plural: i film.

sections.title: Articles and prepositions with articles
sections.summary: Italian has seven forms of 'the' and four of 'a', chosen by the gender, number and first sound of the noun. The common prepositions di, a, da, in and su fuse with the definite article into forms like del, al, nel and sul, which appear in almost every sentence.

rules.title: Masculine singular: il, lo, l'
rules.body: Before most masculine singular nouns the article is il: il libro, il ragazzo, il cane. Before a noun starting with s + consonant, z, gn, ps, pn, x or y, the article is lo: lo studente, lo zaino, lo gnocco, lo psicologo, lo yogurt. Before a vowel it is l' with an apostrophe: l'amico, l'albero, l'uomo. The same first-sound rule chooses uno and the l'-forms of bello and quello later on, so it is worth learning well.

rules.title: Feminine singular: la, l'
rules.body: Feminine singular nouns take la before any consonant, including s + consonant and z: la casa, la studentessa, la zia. Before a vowel la becomes l': l'amica, l'ora, l'isola. The apostrophe form looks the same for both genders, so l'amico (male) and l'amica (female) differ only in the noun ending.

rules.title: Plural articles: i, gli, le
rules.body: Each singular article has a plural partner. il becomes i: i libri, i ragazzi. lo and masculine l' both become gli: gli studenti, gli zaini, gli amici. la and feminine l' both become le: le case, le amiche. The plural articles never take an apostrophe (gli amici, le amiche, not gl'amici), with gli elision now considered old-fashioned.

rules.title: Indefinite articles: un, uno, una, un'
rules.body: The indefinite article follows the same sound rule. Masculine: un before most sounds including vowels, with no apostrophe (un libro, un amico, un uomo), and uno before s + consonant, z, gn, ps, y (uno studente, uno zaino, uno sport). Feminine: una before a consonant (una casa, una studentessa) and un' with an apostrophe before a vowel (un'amica, un'ora). Remember: un amico has no apostrophe because un is the full form; un'amica has one because una has lost its a.

rules.title: When Italian uses 'the' and English does not
rules.body: The definite article is used with nouns in a general sense (Mi piace il caffè: I like coffee; Gli italiani amano il calcio), with languages (studio l'italiano), with possessives (il mio libro), with countries and regions (l'Italia, la Toscana) but not with cities (Roma, Milano), with titles when talking about someone (il signor Rossi, la dottoressa Bianchi) but not when addressing them (Buongiorno, signor Rossi), and with days of the week to mean 'every': il lunedì means on Mondays, while lunedì alone means on Monday.

examples.target: L'Italia è bella, Roma è bella.
examples.en: Italy is beautiful, Rome is beautiful. (country with article, city without)
On Mondays I go to the gym.

rules.title: The simple prepositions
rules.body: The core prepositions are di (of, from, 's), a (to, at, in a city), da (from, at someone's place, since), in (in, to a country or region), con (with), su (on, about), per (for, through, in order to), tra or fra (between, among, in a certain time). di also makes possession (il libro di Marco) and origin (sono di Napoli). da marks the origin point (vengo da Milano) and 'at the place of' (vado dal dentista, sono da Anna).

rules.title: Prepositions fused with the article
rules.body: di, a, da, in and su join with the definite article into one word. di: del, dello, della, dell', dei, degli, delle. a: al, allo, alla, all', ai, agli, alle. da: dal, dallo, dalla, dall', dai, dagli, dalle. in: nel, nello, nella, nell', nei, negli, nelle. su: sul, sullo, sulla, sull', sui, sugli, sulle. Note the doubled l in al, dal, sul forms and the change of in to ne-. con and per do not fuse in modern Italian, although col (con + il) is still heard; tra and fra never do.

examples.en: I am going to the cinema. (a + il)
The keys are in the bag. (in + la)
The cat is on the table. (su + il)
I am going back to my friends' place. (da + gli)

rules.title: di + article for 'some'
rules.body: To say 'some' or 'any' with an uncountable or plural noun, Italian uses di fused with the definite article, the partitive: del pane (some bread), della frutta (some fruit), dello zucchero (some sugar), dell'acqua (some water), dei libri (some books), delle amiche (some friends). It is often simply left out, especially in negatives: Non ho pane. Alternatives are un po' di (a bit of) for singulars and alcuni/alcune or qualche + singular for plurals: alcuni libri, qualche libro.

rules.title: a or in for places
rules.body: Use in with countries, regions, continents and large islands (in Italia, in Toscana, in Europa, in Sicilia) and a with cities and towns (a Roma, a Venezia). Many common places take in without an article: in centro, in città, in banca, in ufficio, in cucina, in piazza, in montagna, in vacanza. Others take a without an article: a casa, a scuola, a letto, a teatro. When the place is specified, the article comes back: nella cucina di Anna, alla scuola di mio figlio. The same forms answer both 'where' and 'where to': sono a Roma, vado a Roma.

examples.en: I live in Italy, in Bologna.

examples.target: Vado in banca e poi a casa.
examples.en: I am going to the bank and then home.
We are on holiday in Sicily.

exercises.explain: libro is masculine and starts with an ordinary consonant, so it takes il.
Masculine nouns beginning with s + consonant take lo: lo studente.
Before a vowel the singular article is l' with an apostrophe: l'amico.

exercises.q: 'lo' is used before masculine nouns that begin with z.
exercises.explain: lo zaino, lo zio, lo zucchero: z triggers lo, like s + consonant.

pairs: masculine singular before s + consonant or z

exercises.q: What is the plural of 'lo zaino' (the backpack)?
exercises.explain: lo always becomes gli in the plural: gli zaini.

exercises.q: What is the plural of "l'amica" (the female friend)?
exercises.explain: Feminine l' becomes le, and -ca becomes -che: le amiche.
The plural of lo is gli: gli studenti.
All feminine plurals take le: le ragazze.
Masculine nouns beginning with z take uno, just as they take lo.

exercises.q: Which indefinite article goes with 'amica' (female friend)?
exercises.explain: Feminine una drops its a before a vowel and takes an apostrophe: un'amica.

exercises.q: 'un amico' is written without an apostrophe.
exercises.explain: un is the full masculine form, so nothing is dropped and no apostrophe is needed.
di fuses with il to give del: il libro del professore.
a + il = al: Vado al cinema.
in changes to ne- and fuses with il: nel.

exercises.q: Il libro è ___ tavolo. (su + il: on the table)
exercises.explain: su + il = sul: sul tavolo.

exercises.q: In modern standard Italian, 'per' fuses with the article: 'per il' is written 'pel'.
exercises.explain: per and con do not fuse in modern Italian (only col survives as an option); pel is archaic.

exercises.en: I live in the centre of the city.

exercises.q: Mi piace ___ caffè. (I like coffee, in general)
exercises.explain: Nouns used in a general sense take the definite article: il caffè.
Countries take in without an article: in Italia, in Francia.
Cities take a without an article: a Roma, a Milano.
The partitive del means 'some' with an uncountable noun: del pane.

exercises.q: 'Il lunedì vado in palestra' means 'On Mondays I go to the gym', that is every Monday.
exercises.explain: The article with a day of the week gives a habitual meaning; lunedì alone would be one particular Monday.

exercises.en: I come back from the station at eight.

exercises.q: You meet Mr Rossi. How do you greet him?
exercises.explain: Titles take the article only when talking about the person, never when addressing them.
in + la = nella: nella borsa.

exercises.q: 'gli' is the plural of both 'lo' and masculine "l'".
exercises.explain: lo studente, gli studenti; l'amico, gli amici: both become gli.

sections.title: The present tense
sections.summary: Italian verbs fall into three groups by their infinitive ending, and the present tense is built by swapping that ending for six personal endings. Because the ending shows who is acting, subject pronouns are usually dropped. This chapter also gives essere, avere and the most common irregular verbs.

rules.title: -are verbs: parlare
rules.body: Most Italian verbs end in -are. Remove -are and add -o, -i, -a, -iamo, -ate, -ano: parlo, parli, parla, parliamo, parlate, parlano. The loro form is stressed on the stem (PARlano), not on the ending. Common -are verbs: abitare (to live), lavorare (to work), mangiare (to eat), studiare (to study), comprare (to buy), guardare (to watch), aspettare (to wait for).

rules.title: -ere verbs: prendere
rules.body: Remove -ere and add -o, -i, -e, -iamo, -ete, -ono: prendo, prendi, prende, prendiamo, prendete, prendono. Only the lui/lei, voi and loro endings differ from -are verbs. Common -ere verbs: vedere (to see), leggere (to read), scrivere (to write), vivere (to live), chiedere (to ask), mettere (to put), credere (to believe), ricevere (to receive). Note the stress: PRENdono, LEGgono.

rules.title: -ire verbs: dormire and the -isc- group
rules.body: Plain -ire verbs take -o, -i, -e, -iamo, -ite, -ono: dormo, dormi, dorme, dormiamo, dormite, dormono (also aprire, partire, sentire, offrire, seguire). A large group inserts -isc- in all forms except noi and voi: finisco, finisci, finisce, finiamo, finite, finiscono. This -isc- group includes capire (to understand), preferire (to prefer), pulire (to clean), spedire (to send), costruire (to build). Dictionaries mark the group; when in doubt, -isc- is the more common pattern.

rules.title: Subject pronouns are usually dropped
rules.body: The pronouns are io, tu, lui (he), lei (she), noi, voi, loro. Because the verb ending already shows the person, they are normally left out: Parlo italiano, not Io parlo italiano. They are used for emphasis or contrast (Io lavoro, tu dormi), after anche (anche io), and to avoid ambiguity in the third person (lui parte, lei resta). Lei with a capital L is the polite 'you' for one person and takes the lui/lei verb form; voi is used for more than one person.

rules.title: essere and avere
rules.body: essere (to be): sono, sei, è, siamo, siete, sono. Note that sono is both 'I am' and 'they are', and è has an accent. avere (to have): ho, hai, ha, abbiamo, avete, hanno, with a silent h that only separates them from o, ai, a, anno. avere is used where English uses 'to be' in many set phrases: ho fame (I am hungry), ho sete (thirsty), ho caldo (hot), ho freddo (cold), ho sonno (sleepy), ho paura (afraid), ho fretta (in a hurry), ho vent'anni (I am twenty), ho ragione (I am right).

examples.en: I am a student; are you Italian?
How old are you? I am twenty.

rules.title: Common irregular verbs: andare, fare, stare, dare
rules.body: Four very frequent -are verbs are irregular. andare (to go): vado, vai, va, andiamo, andate, vanno. fare (to do, to make): faccio, fai, fa, facciamo, fate, fanno. stare (to stay, to be in a state): sto, stai, sta, stiamo, state, stanno, used in Come stai? (How are you?). dare (to give): do, dai, dà, diamo, date, danno. The noi and voi forms are regular in all four except fare.

examples.en: I go to work by bus.
How are you? I am well.

rules.title: Modal verbs and other key irregulars
rules.body: potere (can), volere (want) and dovere (must) are followed directly by an infinitive. potere: posso, puoi, può, possiamo, potete, possono. volere: voglio, vuoi, vuole, vogliamo, volete, vogliono. dovere: devo, devi, deve, dobbiamo, dovete, devono. Other irregulars to know: sapere (so, sai, sa, sappiamo, sapete, sanno), venire (vengo, vieni, viene, veniamo, venite, vengono), uscire (esco, esci, esce, usciamo, uscite, escono), dire (dico, dici, dice, diciamo, dite, dicono), bere (bevo, bevi, beve, beviamo, bevete, bevono).

examples.en: We have to leave at six.

examples.target: Esco con gli amici e bevo una birra.
examples.en: I go out with friends and drink a beer.

rules.title: Spelling adjustments: -care, -gare, -ciare, -giare
rules.body: Verbs in -care and -gare add an h before the endings -i and -iamo to keep the hard sound: cercare gives cerco, cerchi, cerca, cerchiamo, cercate, cercano; pagare gives pago, paghi, paga, paghiamo, pagate, pagano. Verbs in -ciare and -giare do not write a double i: cominciare gives comincio, cominci, comincia, cominciamo; mangiare gives mangio, mangi, mangia, mangiamo. Verbs in -iare with an unstressed i likewise keep a single i: studiare gives studi, studiamo.

rules.title: What the present tense covers
rules.body: One Italian present covers English 'I speak', 'I am speaking' and 'I do speak': Parlo con Anna can be any of these. To stress that an action is happening right now, use stare + gerund: sto parlando, stai mangiando, sta dormendo (gerund: -are gives -ando, -ere and -ire give -endo). The present is also used for the near future with a time expression: Domani parto per Milano (I am leaving for Milan tomorrow). With da it expresses 'have been doing': Studio italiano da due anni (I have been studying Italian for two years).

examples.en: I speak / I am speaking with Anna.
Tomorrow I am leaving for Milan.
I have been studying Italian for two years.

exercises.explain: The io form of an -are verb ends in -o: parlo.
The tu form ends in -i: parli.
The noi form is -iamo for all three conjugations: prendiamo.

exercises.q: 'parlano' (they speak) is stressed on the syllable -la-.
exercises.explain: The loro form is stressed on the stem: PAR-la-no.

exercises.q: Lui ___ fino a tardi. (dormire: he sleeps until late)
exercises.explain: dormire is a plain -ire verb: the lui form is dorme.
finire takes -isc-: finisco, finisci, finisce.
The -isc- is not used in the noi and voi forms: finiamo, finite.

exercises.q: 'capire' takes -isc- in the io, tu, lui/lei and loro forms.
exercises.explain: capisco, capisci, capisce, capiscono; only capiamo and capite lack it.
The io form of essere is sono.
The tu form of avere is hai: Hai fame? (Are you hungry?)

exercises.q: How do you say 'I am twenty years old'?
exercises.explain: Age uses avere, not essere: ho vent'anni.
andare is irregular: vado, vai, va, andiamo, andate, vanno.
The tu form of fare is fai.
fare keeps the full stem in the noi form: facciamo.

exercises.q: Subject pronouns like io and tu are usually left out because the verb ending shows who is acting.
exercises.explain: Parlo already means 'I speak'; io is added only for emphasis or contrast.
The subject pronoun io is used for contrast; me and mi are object forms.
The lui form of potere is può, with an accent.
volere is irregular: voglio, vuoi, vuole, vogliamo, volete, vogliono.

exercises.en: I have to study for the exam.

exercises.explain: -care verbs add h before -i to keep the hard k: cerchi.
-gare verbs add h before -iamo: paghiamo.
-giare verbs do not double the i: mangiamo.

exercises.q: 'Sto mangiando' means 'I am eating' right now.
exercises.explain: stare + gerund stresses an action in progress at this moment.

exercises.q: In 'Domani parto per Milano', the present tense refers to
exercises.explain: With a time word like domani, the present is commonly used for planned future actions.

exercises.en: What do you drink in the morning?

exercises.explain: The voi form of venire is regular: venite.
dire: dico, dici, dice, diciamo, dite, dicono.

exercises.q: 'Lei' with a capital L is the polite 'you' and takes the same verb form as lui and lei.
exercises.explain: Lei parla inglese? uses the third-person singular form parla.

sections.title: Adjectives, possessives and agreement
sections.summary: Italian adjectives change their ending to agree with the noun in gender and number and usually follow it. A few, such as bello and buono, change shape before the noun like the articles. Possessives agree with the thing owned and normally carry the article, except with close family members.

rules.title: Agreement: four-form and two-form adjectives
rules.body: Adjectives ending in -o have four forms: rosso, rossa, rossi, rosse (libro rosso, casa rossa, libri rossi, case rosse). Adjectives ending in -e have two: verde for both singular genders and verdi for both plurals (libro verde, casa verde, libri verdi, case verdi). An adjective describing a mixed group of masculine and feminine nouns takes the masculine plural: Marco e Anna sono simpatici. The same spelling rules as nouns apply: bianco, bianchi; bianca, bianche; simpatico, simpatici.

examples.target: una casa verde, due case verdi
examples.en: a green house, two green houses
Marco and Anna are nice. (masculine plural for a mixed pair)

rules.title: Adjectives usually follow the noun
rules.body: The normal position is after the noun: un gatto nero, una ragazza italiana, un film interessante. Colours, nationalities, shapes, physical descriptions and any adjective with its own modifier always follow (un libro molto bello). A small set of very common adjectives often go before the noun: bello, brutto, buono, cattivo, grande, piccolo, nuovo, vecchio, giovane, stesso, altro. Position can change meaning: un vecchio amico is an old (long-standing) friend, un amico vecchio is an elderly friend; una grande donna is a great woman, una donna grande is a big woman.

rules.title: bello and quello change shape like the definite article
rules.body: Before a noun, bello (beautiful) takes forms that mirror il, lo, l', i, gli, la, le: bel libro, bello studente, bell'uomo, bei libri, begli studenti, begli uomini, bella casa, bell'amica, belle case. quello (that) does the same: quel libro, quello studente, quell'uomo, quei libri, quegli studenti, quella casa, quelle case. After the noun or after essere, bello is regular: il libro è bello, gli uomini sono belli.

examples.target: un bel libro, due bei libri
examples.en: a beautiful book, two beautiful books
These books are beautiful. (regular after the verb)

rules.title: buono, grande and santo before a noun
rules.body: Before a noun, buono follows the pattern of the indefinite article: buon libro, buon amico (like un), buono studente, buono zaino (like uno), buona sera (like una), buon'idea or buona idea before a feminine vowel. Hence buongiorno, buonasera, buon appetito, buon viaggio. grande may shorten to gran before a singular noun starting with a consonant: un gran giorno, una gran fame, but un grande amico. santo becomes san before a masculine name starting with a consonant: San Pietro, San Marco, but Santo Stefano and Sant'Antonio.

examples.en: a good student (buono before s + consonant)

rules.title: Possessives agree with the thing owned and take the article
rules.body: The possessives are mio, tuo, suo, nostro, vostro, loro, each with four forms except loro: il mio, la mia, i miei, le mie; il tuo, la tua, i tuoi, le tue; il suo, la sua, i suoi, le sue; il nostro, la nostra, i nostri, le nostre; il vostro, la vostra, i vostri, le vostre; il loro, la loro, i loro, le loro. They normally come with the definite article and agree with the noun that follows, not with the owner: il suo libro is his book or her book; la sua casa is his or her house. Suo also serves as the polite 'your' (il Suo passaporto).

examples.target: il mio libro, la mia casa
i tuoi amici, le tue amiche

rules.title: No article with singular family members
rules.body: The article is dropped before a possessive with a singular, unmodified family noun: mio padre, mia madre, tuo fratello, sua sorella, nostro zio, vostra nonna. The article comes back in the plural (i miei fratelli, le tue sorelle), always with loro (il loro padre), when the noun is modified (la mia sorella minore, il mio caro nonno), and with affectionate or diminutive forms (la mia mamma, il mio papà, il mio fratellino). I miei on its own means 'my parents'.

examples.target: I miei fratelli vivono a Roma.

examples.en: my younger sister (article because of the adjective)

rules.title: Comparison: più, meno, di and che
rules.body: Comparatives use più (more) or meno (less) before the adjective. The second term is introduced by di when comparing two nouns or pronouns (Roma è più grande di Firenze; Lei è più alta di me) and by che when comparing two adjectives, two infinitives, two quantities or two prepositional phrases (È più simpatico che intelligente; È più facile parlare che scrivere). Equality is (così) ... come or (tanto) ... quanto: Marco è alto come Luca. The superlative adds the article: il più grande, la più bella; 'in' after it is di (il più alto della classe). The absolute superlative replaces the final vowel with -issimo: bellissimo, buonissima.

examples.target: Roma è più grande di Firenze.
È più facile parlare che scrivere.
Luca è il più alto della classe.
examples.en: Luca is the tallest in the class.

rules.title: Irregular comparatives
rules.body: Four adjectives have special comparative forms alongside the regular ones: buono gives migliore (better), cattivo gives peggiore (worse), grande gives maggiore (greater, older), piccolo gives minore (smaller, younger). più buono and più grande are also fine, but migliore and peggiore are the usual words for better and worse. The superlatives are il migliore, il peggiore, il maggiore, il minore, and the absolute forms ottimo, pessimo, massimo, minimo. The adverbs bene and male give meglio (better) and peggio (worse).

examples.target: Questo vino è migliore di quello.
examples.en: This wine is better than that one.
It is the worst film of the year.

rules.title: molto, poco, tanto, troppo: adjective or adverb
rules.body: These words agree with a noun when they describe quantity (adjective use): molti libri, molte case, poca gente, troppi errori, tante amiche. They stay invariable when they modify an adjective, a verb or an adverb (adverb use): Maria è molto bella, i ragazzi sono molto stanchi, mangio troppo, parla poco. A quick test: if 'very' or 'a lot' fits in English, the word is invariable; if 'many' or 'much' fits, it agrees. questo and quello as demonstratives agree in full: questo libro, questa casa, questi libri, queste case.

exercises.explain: casa is feminine singular, so the adjective takes -a: rossa.
Masculine plural noun, masculine plural adjective: nuovi.
-e adjectives take -i for any plural: le macchine verdi.

exercises.q: Adjectives ending in -e have the same form for masculine and feminine.
exercises.explain: verde, grande, intelligente serve both genders; only the plural changes to -i.

exercises.q: How do you say 'a black cat'?
exercises.explain: Colour adjectives follow the noun and agree: gatto nero.

exercises.q: Adjectives of colour and nationality normally come after the noun.
exercises.explain: una macchina rossa, un ragazzo italiano: these never go before the noun.
Before a masculine noun that takes il, bello becomes bel.
occhi takes gli, so bello takes the matching form begli.
studente takes lo, so the matching form is bello.
Before a masculine noun that takes un, buono shortens to buon: buongiorno.
sera is feminine and starts with a consonant, so buona, like una.

exercises.q: 'un vecchio amico' and 'un amico vecchio' mean exactly the same thing.
exercises.explain: Before the noun vecchio means long-standing; after it, it means elderly.
Possessives take the definite article and agree with the noun: il mio libro.
casa is feminine singular, so tuo becomes tua.
The masculine plural of suo is suoi: i suoi amici.
Possessives agree with the thing owned, not the owner, so il suo libro is his or her book.
Singular, unmodified family members take no article: mio padre.
madre is a singular family noun, so no article: sua madre.
In the plural the article returns: i miei fratelli.

exercises.q: 'il loro padre' is correct with the article, because loro always keeps it.
exercises.explain: loro is the one possessive that never drops the article, even with family: il loro padre.

exercises.answer: Mia sorella è più alta di me.
exercises.en: My sister is taller than me.

exercises.explain: When comparing two nouns, 'than' is di: più grande di Firenze.
buono has the irregular comparative migliore: questo vino è migliore.

exercises.q: How do you say 'very good' with the -issimo ending?
exercises.explain: Drop the final vowel and add -issimo: buon + issimo.

exercises.q: In 'Maria è molto bella', molto stays invariable because it is an adverb.
exercises.explain: molto modifying an adjective means 'very' and does not agree.
molto as an adjective agrees with ragazze: molte ragazze.

exercises.q: un ___ giorno (grande, shortened before a consonant)
exercises.explain: grande may shorten to gran before a singular noun beginning with a consonant: un gran giorno.

sections.title: The passato prossimo
sections.summary: The passato prossimo is the everyday past tense of spoken Italian, covering English 'I ate', 'I have eaten' and 'I did eat'. It is built from avere or essere plus a past participle, and the choice of auxiliary decides whether the participle must agree with the subject.

rules.title: Formation: auxiliary + past participle
rules.body: The passato prossimo combines the present of avere or essere with the past participle. Regular participles are formed from the infinitive: -are gives -ato (parlare, parlato), -ere gives -uto (vendere, venduto; avere, avuto), -ire gives -ito (dormire, dormito; finire, finito). Ho parlato means I spoke, I have spoken or I did speak; Italian makes no difference between these.

rules.title: avere with most verbs; the participle does not change
rules.body: Most verbs, and all verbs that can take a direct object, use avere. With avere the participle keeps its -o ending whoever the subject is: Maria ha mangiato, i ragazzi hanno mangiato, le ragazze hanno mangiato. The only exception, covered below, is when a direct object pronoun comes before the verb. Common avere verbs: mangiare, bere, comprare, vedere, leggere, scrivere, fare, dire, prendere, dormire, lavorare, studiare, parlare, telefonare.

rules.title: essere with movement, change and reflexives; the participle agrees
rules.body: Verbs of movement and of change of state, plus a few others, take essere: andare, venire, arrivare, partire, uscire, entrare, tornare, salire, scendere, cadere, nascere, morire, crescere, diventare, restare, rimanere, stare, essere itself, succedere, piacere. All reflexive verbs also take essere (mi sono alzato). With essere the participle agrees with the subject like an adjective: Marco è andato, Maria è andata, i ragazzi sono andati, le ragazze sono andate.

examples.target: I ragazzi sono partiti alle otto.

rules.title: Agreement with avere after lo, la, li, le and ne
rules.body: When a direct object pronoun lo, la, li or le comes before a verb with avere, the participle agrees with that pronoun: Hai visto Maria? Sì, l'ho vista. Hai comprato i libri? Sì, li ho comprati. Hai mangiato le mele? Sì, le ho mangiate. The same happens with ne when it stands for a quantity: Quante mele hai mangiato? Ne ho mangiate tre. With mi, ti, ci, vi the agreement is optional, and with indirect pronouns there is never any agreement.

examples.en: I bought them (m.) at the market.

rules.title: Irregular past participles
rules.body: Many common verbs, mostly in -ere, have irregular participles that must be learned: fare, fatto; dire, detto; leggere, letto; scrivere, scritto; vedere, visto; prendere, preso; mettere, messo; aprire, aperto; offrire, offerto; chiudere, chiuso; chiedere, chiesto; rispondere, risposto; bere, bevuto; vivere, vissuto; scegliere, scelto; decidere, deciso; perdere, perso; vincere, vinto; conoscere, conosciuto; venire, venuto; essere and stare, stato; nascere, nato; morire, morto; rimanere, rimasto; piacere, piaciuto; succedere, successo.

examples.en: I was born in Naples. (female speaker)

rules.title: Verbs that take either auxiliary
rules.body: Some verbs take avere when they have a direct object and essere when they do not: finire, cominciare, cambiare, passare, salire, scendere, correre. Ho finito il libro (I finished the book) but Il film è finito (The film ended). Ho cominciato la lezione but La lezione è cominciata. Ho passato un bel weekend but Sono passato da Marco (I dropped by Marco's). The modals dovere, potere and volere formally take the auxiliary of the infinitive that follows (sono dovuto partire, ho dovuto lavorare), though avere is widely used in speech for both.

examples.target: Ho passato le vacanze al mare.
examples.en: I spent the holidays at the seaside.

rules.title: non, mai, già, ancora and sempre
rules.body: non goes before the auxiliary: Non ho capito. Non siamo andati. The short adverbs mai (ever, never), già (already), ancora (yet, still), sempre (always), appena (just) and più (any more) normally sit between the auxiliary and the participle: Non ho mai visto Roma. Ho già mangiato. Non ho ancora finito. Ho sempre lavorato qui. Sono appena arrivato. Non ci sono più andato. In questions, mai means 'ever': Hai mai mangiato la pizza napoletana?

examples.target: Hai mai mangiato la pizza napoletana?
examples.en: Have you ever eaten Neapolitan pizza?

rules.title: Time expressions for the past
rules.body: Typical markers that go with the passato prossimo: ieri (yesterday), ieri sera (last night), l'altro ieri (the day before yesterday), stamattina (this morning), la settimana scorsa (last week), il mese scorso, l'anno scorso, sabato scorso, due giorni fa (two days ago), un'ora fa, molto tempo fa. fa follows the time expression, like English 'ago'. These usually come at the start or end of the sentence: Ieri ho lavorato; Ho lavorato ieri.

examples.target: Stamattina ho fatto colazione al bar.
examples.en: This morning I had breakfast at the café.

exercises.q: What is the past participle of 'parlare'?
exercises.explain: -are verbs form the participle in -ato: parlato.
Regular -are participle: mangiato; with avere it never changes.

exercises.q: What is the past participle of 'dormire'?
exercises.explain: -ire verbs form the participle in -ito: dormito.

exercises.q: Regular -ere verbs form their past participle in -uto.
exercises.explain: vendere gives venduto, avere gives avuto, credere gives creduto.
comprare takes avere, and the subject Maria needs the lui/lei form ha.
The noi form of avere is abbiamo: abbiamo visto.
andare is a verb of movement and takes essere: è andata.

exercises.q: 'andare' takes essere in the passato prossimo.
exercises.explain: Verbs of movement like andare, venire, arrivare and partire take essere.
With essere the participle agrees with the masculine plural subject: partiti.
Feminine plural subject with essere: arrivate.

exercises.q: With avere the participle agrees with the subject, so 'Maria ha mangiata la pizza' is correct.
exercises.explain: With avere the participle stays in -o unless a direct object pronoun precedes: Maria ha mangiato la pizza.
aprire has the irregular participle aperto.

exercises.q: What is the past participle of 'prendere'?
exercises.explain: prendere is irregular: preso.

exercises.answer: Ieri sera abbiamo mangiato al ristorante.
exercises.en: Last night we ate at the restaurant.

exercises.q: ___ nato nel 1990. (I was born; male speaker)
exercises.explain: nascere takes essere: sono nato.

exercises.q: Marco è ___ a casa tutto il giorno. (stare)
exercises.explain: stare takes essere and has the participle stato, agreeing with Marco.

exercises.q: 'essere' uses essere as its own auxiliary, and its participle is 'stato'.
exercises.explain: Sono stato a Roma: essere borrows the participle stato and takes essere.
The direct object pronoun la (l') precedes the verb, so the participle agrees: mangiata.
li before avere makes the participle masculine plural: letti.

exercises.q: In 'Non ho mai visto Roma', mai goes between the auxiliary and the participle.
exercises.explain: Short adverbs like mai, già and ancora sit between ho and the participle.
fa follows the time expression and means 'ago': due giorni fa.

exercises.q: Mi ___ alzato alle sette. (I got up)
exercises.explain: Reflexive verbs always take essere: mi sono alzato.

exercises.answer: Non siamo ancora arrivati a casa.

exercises.explain: bere has the participle bevuto.
finire with a direct object (il libro) takes avere: ha finito.

exercises.q: 'Il film è finito' uses essere because finire has no direct object here.
exercises.explain: finire takes avere with an object and essere without one.
nascere takes essere, and the feminine participle nata agrees with Anna.

exercises.q: What is the past participle of 'vivere'?
exercises.explain: vivere is irregular: vissuto; visto is the participle of vedere.

exercises.answer: Hai mai mangiato la pasta al pesto?
exercises.en: Have you ever eaten pasta with pesto?

sections.title: Imperfetto vs passato prossimo, and the future
sections.summary: The imperfetto describes how things were and what used to happen, while the passato prossimo reports what happened; choosing between them is the key skill of Italian past narration. The future tense is regular for most verbs, with a dozen shortened stems to memorise.

rules.title: Forms of the imperfetto
rules.body: Drop -re from the infinitive and add -vo, -vi, -va, -vamo, -vate, -vano: parlare gives parlavo, parlavi, parlava, parlavamo, parlavate, parlavano; prendere gives prendevo, prendevi, prendeva, prendevamo, prendevate, prendevano; dormire gives dormivo, dormivi, dormiva, dormivamo, dormivate, dormivano. Almost every verb is regular, including andare (andavo), avere (avevo) and the -isc- verbs (finivo). The loro form is stressed on the stem: parLAvano.

examples.en: As a child I spoke only dialect.
We always used to take the train.
They were sleeping when I arrived.

rules.title: Irregular imperfetto: essere, fare, dire, bere
rules.body: essere is the only truly irregular verb: ero, eri, era, eravamo, eravate, erano. Three others use an older, longer stem: fare gives facevo, facevi, faceva, facevamo, facevate, facevano; dire gives dicevo, dicevi, diceva...; bere gives bevevo, bevevi, beveva.... Verbs in -urre and -orre do the same: tradurre, traducevo; porre, ponevo.

examples.en: What were you doing last night?

rules.title: What the imperfetto is for
rules.body: Use the imperfetto for habits and repeated actions in the past (Da bambina andavo al mare ogni estate: I used to go), for descriptions of people, places, weather and feelings (Era una bella giornata; Mio nonno aveva i capelli bianchi; Avevo paura), for age and time in the past (Avevo dieci anni; Erano le otto), for mental states (Volevo, sapevo, pensavo, credevo), and for an action in progress that forms the background to another (Mentre dormivo...). English equivalents are 'used to', 'was ...ing' and the plain past of state verbs.

examples.target: Da bambina andavo al mare ogni estate.
examples.en: As a little girl I used to go to the seaside every summer.

examples.target: Era una bella giornata e faceva caldo.
examples.en: It was a lovely day and it was hot.

examples.target: Erano le otto quando sono uscito.
examples.en: It was eight o'clock when I went out.
I didn't know you were ill.

rules.title: Choosing between the two tenses
rules.body: The passato prossimo reports a completed event, something that happened once or a specific number of times, often with a clear start or end: Ieri ho mangiato la pizza; Sono andato a Roma tre volte. The imperfetto paints the setting or an ongoing or habitual situation with no attention to its end. The two meet in one sentence when an event interrupts a background: Mentre dormivo, è suonato il telefono (While I was sleeping, the phone rang). Two simultaneous backgrounds are both imperfetto: Mentre io cucinavo, lui leggeva.

examples.target: Da studente mangiavo spesso la pizza.
examples.en: As a student I often ate pizza. (habit)

examples.target: Mentre dormivo, è suonato il telefono.
examples.en: While I was sleeping, the phone rang.

rules.title: Verbs that change meaning: sapere, conoscere, volere, potere, dovere
rules.body: With state verbs the tense shifts the meaning. sapevo = I knew, ho saputo = I found out. conoscevo = I knew (a person or place), ho conosciuto = I met for the first time. volevo = I wanted, ho voluto = I insisted and did. non volevo = I didn't feel like it, non ho voluto = I refused. potevo = I was able (in principle), ho potuto = I managed to. dovevo = I was supposed to, ho dovuto = I had to and did.

examples.en: I didn't know you were here.
I found out the news yesterday.

rules.title: Forms of the future
rules.body: The future is built on the infinitive minus its final -e, with -are verbs changing that a to e: parlare gives parlerò, parlerai, parlerà, parleremo, parlerete, parleranno; prendere gives prenderò, prenderai, prenderà, prenderemo, prenderete, prenderanno; dormire gives dormirò, dormirai, dormirà, dormiremo, dormirete, dormiranno. The io and lui/lei forms end in a written accent. The spelling rules apply: -care and -gare keep an h (cercherò, pagherò), -ciare and -giare drop the i (comincerò, mangerò).

examples.en: Tomorrow I will speak to the manager.
We will take the nine o'clock train.

rules.title: Irregular future stems
rules.body: Some verbs shorten their stem but keep the regular endings. Dropped vowel: avere, avrò; andare, andrò; potere, potrò; dovere, dovrò; sapere, saprò; vedere, vedrò; vivere, vivrò. Double r: venire, verrò; volere, vorrò; rimanere, rimarrò; bere, berrò; tenere, terrò. Stem without e-change: fare, farò; dare, darò; stare, starò. essere has its own stem: sarò, sarai, sarà, saremo, sarete, saranno.

examples.en: I will be home at six.
What will you do this summer?

rules.title: Uses of the future
rules.body: The future is used for plans, promises and predictions: L'anno prossimo andrò in Italia; Ti chiamerò; Domani pioverà. After quando, se, appena and non appena, Italian uses the future where English uses the present: Quando arriverò, ti chiamerò; Se avrò tempo, verrò. It also expresses probability or a guess about the present: Sarà a casa (he is probably at home); Che ore sono? Saranno le dieci. For near, fixed plans the present is more common in speech: Domani parto.

examples.en: Next year I will go to Italy.
When I arrive, I'll call you.

examples.target: Dove sarà Marco? Sarà in ufficio.
examples.en: Where can Marco be? He is probably at the office.
If I have time, I'll come.

exercises.explain: The io form of the imperfetto is -vo: parlavo.

exercises.q: Da bambino ___ a calcio ogni giorno. (giocare, io)
exercises.explain: A past habit takes the imperfetto: giocavo.
The noi form is -vamo: avevamo.

exercises.q: The imperfetto of essere is regular: essevo, essevi, esseva.
exercises.explain: essere is irregular: ero, eri, era, eravamo, eravate, erano.

exercises.q: Quando ___ giovani, abitavano a Roma. (essere, loro)
exercises.explain: The loro form of the imperfetto of essere is erano.

exercises.q: Ieri ___ un bel film. (a single completed event)
exercises.explain: A completed one-off event in the past takes the passato prossimo: ho visto.

exercises.q: Da piccolo ___ sempre al mare. (a habit)
exercises.explain: A repeated past habit takes the imperfetto: andavo.

exercises.q: The imperfetto is used for descriptions and habitual actions in the past.
exercises.explain: Era una bella giornata; andavo al mare ogni estate.

exercises.answer: Mentre dormivo, è suonato il telefono.
exercises.en: While I was sleeping, the phone rang.

exercises.q: ___ le otto quando sono uscito. (It was eight o'clock)
exercises.explain: Time in the past takes the imperfetto, plural with le otto: erano.
Weather descriptions in the past take the imperfetto: faceva freddo.

exercises.q: Non ___ che eri malato. (I didn't know)
exercises.explain: A state of knowledge is imperfetto: sapevo; ho saputo would mean 'I found out'.

exercises.q: 'Ho conosciuto Maria a Roma' means 'I met Maria for the first time in Rome'.
exercises.explain: In the passato prossimo conoscere means to meet; conoscevo means I already knew.
-are becomes -er- and the io ending is -ò with an accent: parlerò.
The noi future ending is -emo on the stem partir-: partiremo.
The tu future ending is -ai: prenderai.

exercises.q: In the future tense, -are verbs change the a of the infinitive to e: parlare, parlerò.
exercises.explain: parlerò, mangerò, cercherò: the a becomes e before the future endings.
essere has the irregular future stem sar-: sarò.

exercises.q: What is the io future of 'avere'?
exercises.explain: avere drops the e of its stem: avrò, avrai, avrà.
venire has the double-r stem verr-: verranno.
-gare keeps the hard g with an h: pagheremo.
-giare drops the i before the future ending: mangerò.

exercises.en: When I arrive, I'll call you.

exercises.q: 'Sarà a casa' can mean 'He is probably at home'.
exercises.explain: The future expresses a guess about the present: sarà = he must be, he is probably.

exercises.q: Dove ___ Marco? Non risponde al telefono. (a guess)
exercises.explain: The future of probability: Dove sarà? = Where can he be?
andare drops a vowel in the future: andrò.

exercises.en: As a little girl I had a dog.

exercises.q: After 'quando' and 'se' referring to the future, Italian uses the future tense where English uses the present.
exercises.explain: Quando arriverò, ti chiamerò: both verbs are in the future.
-ire verbs keep the i in the imperfetto: dormivo.

sections.title: Pronouns: direct, indirect, ne and ci
sections.summary: Italian object pronouns go before the conjugated verb or attach to an infinitive, and indirect and direct pronouns combine into forms like glielo. The little words ne and ci replace phrases with di and a, and the verb piacere reverses the English order of liker and thing liked.

rules.title: Direct object pronouns
rules.body: The direct object pronouns are mi (me), ti (you), lo (him, it), la (her, it), ci (us), vi (you plural), li (them, masculine), le (them, feminine); La with a capital is the polite 'you'. They go directly before the conjugated verb: Lo vedo (I see him), La conosco (I know her), Ci aspettano (They are waiting for us). lo and la shorten to l' before a vowel or h: l'aspetto, l'ho visto; li and le never shorten.

examples.en: Do you see Marco? Yes, I see him.

examples.target: Compro la frutta. La compro al mercato.
examples.en: I buy fruit. I buy it at the market.
I have been waiting for him/her for an hour.

rules.title: Indirect object pronouns
rules.body: The indirect pronouns answer 'to whom': mi, ti, gli (to him), le (to her, and Le to you polite), ci, vi, gli (to them; the formal alternative loro follows the verb: parlo loro). They are used with verbs that take a before a person: telefonare a, parlare a, scrivere a, dare a, dire a, chiedere a, rispondere a, regalare a, piacere a. Only gli, le and loro differ from the direct forms, so it matters to know which verbs are indirect: Le telefono (I phone her), Gli scrivo (I write to him).

examples.en: I phone Maria. I phone her.
I write to Marco. I write to him.
I asked them (or him) a favour.

rules.title: Where the pronoun goes
rules.body: Before a conjugated verb, including the auxiliary of the passato prossimo: Lo compro; L'ho comprato; Non lo voglio. With an infinitive the pronoun attaches to its end after the final -e is dropped: comprarlo, vederla, parlargli. After a modal there is a choice: Voglio vederlo or Lo voglio vedere, both correct. Pronouns also attach to the gerund (vedendolo), to ecco (eccolo, eccomi) and to the tu, noi and voi imperatives (compralo, scrivimi).

examples.en: I want to see it. (both orders)
Here he is! / Here it is!

rules.title: ne: of it, of them, some
rules.body: ne replaces a phrase introduced by di or an unstated quantity: Quanti fratelli hai? Ne ho due (I have two of them). Vuoi del pane? Ne voglio un po'. Parliamo di politica? Sì, ne parliamo spesso. It is compulsory when a number or quantity is left standing without its noun: Ne prendo tre, not Prendo tre. In the passato prossimo the participle agrees with what ne stands for: Quante mele hai mangiato? Ne ho mangiate due. ne also means 'from there': Ne vengo adesso.

examples.target: Quanti fratelli hai? Ne ho due.
examples.en: How many brothers do you have? I have two.

examples.target: Vuoi del vino? Sì, ne voglio un bicchiere.
examples.en: Do you want some wine? Yes, I'd like a glass (of it).

rules.title: ci: there, and phrases with a
rules.body: ci stands for a place already mentioned, replacing a, in or su + place: Vai a Roma? Sì, ci vado domani. Sei mai stato in Sicilia? No, non ci sono mai stato. It also replaces a + thing after verbs like pensare a, credere a, riuscire a: Pensi all'esame? Sì, ci penso sempre. Ci penso io means I'll take care of it. The forms c'è and ci sono mean there is and there are: C'è un problema; Ci sono molti turisti. Notice that ci is also the pronoun 'us' and the reflexive 'ourselves'; context tells them apart.

examples.target: Vai a Roma? Sì, ci vado domani.
examples.en: Are you going to Rome? Yes, I'm going (there) tomorrow.

rules.title: Combined pronouns: me lo, te la, glielo
rules.body: When an indirect and a direct pronoun meet, the indirect comes first and changes its i to e: mi + lo = me lo, ti + la = te la, ci + li = ce li, vi + le = ve le, and the same with ne (me ne, te ne, ce ne, ve ne). gli and le both become glie- and join into one word: glielo, gliela, glieli, gliele, gliene, which therefore mean 'it to him', 'it to her' or 'it to them'. Reflexive si does the same: se lo (he buys it for himself). The pair goes before the verb or attaches as a unit: Me lo dai? Puoi darmelo?

examples.target: Mi dai il libro? Sì, te lo do.
examples.en: Will you give me the book? Yes, I'll give it to you.
Can you give it to me?

rules.title: piacere works backwards
rules.body: piacere means 'to be pleasing', so the thing liked is the subject and the person is an indirect object: Mi piace la pizza (pizza is pleasing to me), Mi piacciono gli spaghetti (plural subject, plural verb). Use piace with a singular noun or an infinitive (Mi piace cantare) and piacciono with a plural noun. With a name, use a: A Marco piace il calcio; A Luisa piacciono i gatti. In the passato prossimo piacere takes essere and the participle agrees with the thing liked: Il film mi è piaciuto; La pizza mi è piaciuta; I libri mi sono piaciuti. Verbs that behave the same way: mancare (to be missed), servire (to be needed), interessare, sembrare, bastare.

examples.target: Il film mi è piaciuto molto.
examples.en: I liked the film a lot.

rules.title: Stressed pronouns and reflexive pronouns
rules.body: After a preposition, and for emphasis, Italian uses the stressed forms me, te, lui, lei, noi, voi, loro (and Lei polite): con me, per te, a lui, da noi, secondo loro. They can also replace an unstressed pronoun to highlight it: Cerco te, non lui. Reflexive pronouns are mi, ti, si, ci, vi, si and go in the same positions as object pronouns: mi alzo (I get up), ti chiami (you are called), si lava (he washes), ci vediamo (we'll see each other), with the infinitive alzarsi, chiamarsi.

examples.target: Mi chiamo Anna e mi alzo alle sette.
examples.en: My name is Anna and I get up at seven.

exercises.explain: Marco is a masculine direct object, so lo.
la frutta is feminine singular, replaced by the direct pronoun la.

exercises.q: Conosci i miei amici? Sì, ___ conosco.
exercises.explain: i miei amici is masculine plural, so li.

exercises.q: Direct object pronouns go before a conjugated verb.
exercises.explain: Lo vedo, la conosco, li aspetto: the pronoun precedes the verb.
telefonare a takes an indirect object; 'to her' is le.
The indirect pronoun 'to him' is gli.

exercises.q: Hai parlato ai ragazzi? Sì, ___ ho parlato.
exercises.explain: parlare a is indirect, and in everyday Italian 'to them' is gli.

exercises.q: 'gli' is used for 'to him' and, in everyday Italian, also for 'to them'.
exercises.explain: Gli scrivo can mean I write to him or to them; the formal loro follows the verb.

exercises.q: Voglio ___. (I want to see it, masculine)
exercises.explain: The infinitive drops its final -e and the pronoun attaches: vederlo.

exercises.q: 'Lo voglio vedere' and 'Voglio vederlo' are both correct.
exercises.explain: With a modal the pronoun may precede the verb or attach to the infinitive.
Pronouns attach to ecco: eccola.
A quantity without its noun needs ne: Ne ho due (I have two of them).

exercises.q: Vuoi del pane? Sì, ___ voglio un po'.
exercises.explain: ne stands for 'of it' (del pane): ne voglio un po'.

exercises.q: 'ne' replaces a phrase introduced by 'di' or a quantity of something.
exercises.explain: Ne parliamo (we talk about it); Ne prendo tre (I take three of them).

exercises.q: Vai a Roma? Sì, ___ vado domani.
exercises.explain: ci replaces a + place: ci vado = I go there.

exercises.q: ___ sono molti studenti in classe. (there are)
exercises.explain: 'There are' is ci sono; 'there is' is c'è.

exercises.q: Mi dai il libro? Sì, ___ do.
exercises.explain: ti becomes te before lo: te lo do.

exercises.q: Dai la penna a Marco? Sì, ___ do.
exercises.explain: gli + la fuse into gliela (it, feminine, to him).

exercises.q: Mi porti le chiavi? Sì, ___ porto. (them to you)
exercises.explain: ti + le = te le: te le porto.

exercises.q: Before lo, la, li, le and ne, the pronoun mi becomes me and gli becomes glie-.
exercises.explain: me lo, te lo, glielo, ce lo, ve lo: the indirect pronoun changes its vowel.
la pizza is singular, so the verb is piace.
gli spaghetti is plural, so the verb is piacciono.
il calcio is singular: piace; the liker is introduced by a.

exercises.q: 'Mi piace' literally means 'it is pleasing to me', so the thing liked is the grammatical subject.
exercises.explain: That is why the verb agrees with the thing liked: mi piace / mi piacciono.
piacere takes essere, and the participle agrees with il film: piaciuto.
After a preposition the stressed form me is used: con me.

sections.title: Questions, negation and the imperative
sections.summary: Italian asks yes/no questions by intonation alone, puts non before the verb and happily stacks negatives like non ... mai. The imperative has separate forms for tu, Lei, noi and voi, and the position of pronouns depends on which one you use.

rules.title: Yes/no questions by intonation
rules.body: A statement becomes a question simply by raising the voice at the end, with no change of word order and no helper like English 'do': Parli italiano? Hai fame? Maria viene stasera? The subject, if expressed, may also move to the end for a more neutral question: Viene Maria stasera? Short answers are Sì or No, often with the verb repeated: Sì, parlo italiano. No, non ho fame. A tag question adds vero?, no? or giusto?: Sei italiano, vero?

rules.title: Question words
rules.body: chi (who), che cosa, cosa or che (what), dove (where), quando (when), perché (why; also 'because'), come (how), quanto (how much) and quale (which). The question word usually comes first and is followed directly by the verb: Dove abiti? Quando parti? quanto agrees when it is an adjective: quanti libri, quante ragazze; quale has the plural quali. Before è, dove, come and cosa drop their final vowel: Dov'è? Com'è? Cos'è? Note that qual è is written without an apostrophe.

rules.title: Prepositions stay with the question word
rules.body: Unlike English, Italian never leaves a preposition at the end of a question. It goes before the question word: Con chi parli? (Who are you talking to?), Di dove sei? (Where are you from?), A che ora parte il treno? (What time does the train leave?), Per chi è questo regalo? (Who is this present for?), Di che cosa parlate? (What are you talking about?).

examples.en: Who are you going to the cinema with?

rules.title: Negation with non
rules.body: Put non immediately before the verb, and before any object pronouns attached to it: Non capisco. Non lo so. Non mi piace. Non ho mangiato. The answer no is followed by a comma and a full negative sentence: No, non sono italiano. non also goes before the auxiliary in the passato prossimo and before a modal: Non posso venire. Non ho capito.

rules.title: Double negatives: non ... mai, niente, nessuno, più
rules.body: Italian keeps non and adds a second negative word after the verb; this is correct, not sloppy: non ... mai (never), non ... niente or nulla (nothing), non ... nessuno (nobody, no one), non ... più (no longer, no more), non ... ancora (not yet), non ... neanche, nemmeno or neppure (not even), non ... né ... né (neither ... nor). Non mangio mai la carne. Non vedo nessuno. Non c'è niente. When the negative word starts the sentence, non is dropped: Nessuno è venuto. Niente è impossibile. Mai!

examples.en: Nobody came. (no non when nessuno comes first)

rules.title: The tu imperative
rules.body: The informal command to one person uses the present tense forms, except that -are verbs end in -a: parlare gives Parla! (not parli), prendere gives Prendi!, dormire gives Dormi!, finire gives Finisci!. The negative tu imperative is non + infinitive: Non parlare! Non mangiare! Non aprire la finestra! Five common verbs have short forms: andare, va' (or vai); fare, fa' (or fai); dare, da' (or dai); stare, sta' (or stai); dire, di'. essere gives Sii!, avere gives Abbi!, sapere gives Sappi!.

examples.target: Va' a casa! Di' la verità!

rules.title: The Lei, noi and voi imperatives
rules.body: The polite Lei imperative swaps the vowel: -are verbs take -i (Parli! Aspetti! Scusi!), -ere and -ire verbs take -a (Prenda! Senta! Finisca! Apra!). Its negative simply adds non: Non parli! Common irregulars: sia (essere), abbia (avere), vada (andare), faccia (fare), dica (dire), venga (venire), stia (stare), dia (dare), esca (uscire), beva (bere). The noi and voi imperatives are the same as the present: Andiamo! (Let's go), Parliamo! Parlate! Venite! Their negatives are non + the same form: Non parlate! Non andiamo!

examples.en: Excuse me, madam, do take one.
Listen, tell me! (polite, typical of shops)

rules.title: Pronouns with the imperative
rules.body: With the tu, noi and voi imperatives, object and reflexive pronouns attach to the end of the verb: Compralo! (Buy it), Scrivimi! (Write to me), Alzati! (Get up), Diteglielo! (Tell him). After the short forms va', fa', da', sta', di' the pronoun's first consonant doubles: dammi (give me), dimmi (tell me), fallo (do it), vacci (go there), stammi bene; gli does not double: dagli, digli. In the negative tu form the pronoun may attach or precede: Non farlo! or Non lo fare! With the Lei imperative the pronoun always goes before the verb: Mi dica! Si accomodi! Lo prenda!

examples.en: Please sit down, sir. (Lei: pronoun before the verb)

exercises.q: How do you turn 'Parli italiano.' into a yes/no question?
options: Keep the same words and raise the intonation: Parli italiano?
Add a helper verb: Fai parli italiano?
Put the verb at the end: Italiano parli?
Add 'sì' at the end: Parli italiano sì?
exercises.explain: Italian yes/no questions use intonation alone, with no change of word order.

exercises.q: Italian yes/no questions do not need an auxiliary like English 'do'.
exercises.explain: Hai fame? means Are you hungry?; the statement and the question have the same words.

exercises.q: ___ è il bagno? (Where is the bathroom? Use the shortened form before è)
exercises.explain: dove drops its final e before è: Dov'è il bagno?
As an adverb with a verb, quanto is invariable: Quanto costa?

exercises.q: ___ libri hai? (How many books do you have?)
exercises.explain: quanto agrees with libri, masculine plural: quanti.

exercises.q: ___ ore sono? (What time is it? Literally 'what hours are they')
exercises.explain: The set phrase is Che ore sono? (or Che ora è?).

exercises.q: How do you say 'Who are you going with?'
exercises.explain: The preposition goes before the question word: Con chi.

exercises.q: In Italian a preposition can be left at the end of a question, as in English 'Who are you talking to?'
exercises.explain: The preposition must precede the question word: Con chi parli?
The verb is negated with non; no is only the answer word.
non comes first, then the pronoun, then the verb: Non lo so.

exercises.q: 'non' goes before the verb and before any object pronouns that precede it: Non lo vedo.
exercises.explain: The order is non + pronoun + verb.
non ... mai means never; niente is nothing, nessuno is nobody, più is no longer.
non ... nessuno means nobody: Non c'è nessuno.
When the negative word opens the sentence, non is dropped: Nessuno è venuto.

exercises.q: Double negatives such as 'non ... niente' are standard Italian, not a mistake.
exercises.explain: Non ho capito niente is the normal way to say I didn't understand anything.

exercises.q: What is the tu imperative of 'parlare'?
exercises.explain: -are verbs take -a in the tu imperative: Parla!

exercises.q: What is the tu imperative of 'prendere'?
exercises.explain: -ere verbs use the present tu form: Prendi!

exercises.q: ___ la porta! (aprire, tu: open the door)
exercises.explain: -ire verbs use the present tu form: Apri!

exercises.q: What is the Lei (polite) imperative of 'parlare'?
exercises.explain: The Lei imperative of -are verbs ends in -i: Parli!
The Lei imperative of -ere verbs ends in -a: Prenda!

exercises.q: The negative tu imperative is non + infinitive: Non parlare!
exercises.explain: Non mangiare! Non aprire!: the infinitive replaces the imperative after non.
The tu imperative of venire is Vieni; Venga is the Lei form.

exercises.q: Mi ___ un caffè, per favore. (Lei: give me)
exercises.explain: The Lei imperative of dare is dia: Mi dia un caffè.

exercises.q: ___ la verità! (dire + mi, tu: tell me)
exercises.explain: di' + mi doubles the m: Dimmi!

exercises.q: With the tu imperative, where does an object pronoun go?
options: Attached to the end of the verb: Fallo!
exercises.explain: Pronouns attach to tu, noi and voi imperatives: Fallo, compralo, scrivimi.

exercises.q: With the Lei imperative the pronoun is attached to the end: 'Dicami!'
exercises.explain: With Lei the pronoun goes before the verb: Mi dica!

sections.title: Numbers, time, dates and politeness
sections.summary: This chapter gives the numbers and the patterns for prices, ages, clock time and dates, then the social grammar of Italian: when to use tu or Lei, how to address people with titles, and the greetings and formulas you will hear every day.

rules.title: Numbers 0 to 20
rules.body: zero, uno, due, tre, quattro, cinque, sei, sette, otto, nove, dieci, undici, dodici, tredici, quattordici, quindici, sedici, diciassette, diciotto, diciannove, venti. uno behaves like the indefinite article before a noun (un libro, una casa, uno studente); all other numbers are invariable. Numbers come before the noun and the noun is plural from two upwards: due libri, tre case.

rules.title: Tens, hundreds and thousands
rules.body: venti, trenta, quaranta, cinquanta, sessanta, settanta, ottanta, novanta, cento. Compounds are written as one word: ventidue, trentacinque, novantanove. Before uno and otto the ten drops its final vowel: ventuno, ventotto, trentuno, quarantotto. tre takes an accent at the end of a compound: ventitré, quarantatré. cento is invariable (duecento, trecento), mille becomes mila in the plural (duemila, diecimila), and milione is a noun that needs di before another noun: un milione di euro, due milioni di abitanti. Years are read as full numbers: 1999 is millenovecentonovantanove, 2024 is duemilaventiquattro.

rules.title: Ordinal numbers
rules.body: The first ten ordinals are irregular: primo, secondo, terzo, quarto, quinto, sesto, settimo, ottavo, nono, decimo. From eleven on, drop the final vowel of the cardinal and add -esimo: undicesimo, dodicesimo, ventesimo, ventunesimo, centesimo; numbers ending in -tré and -sei keep the vowel: ventitreesimo, ventiseiesimo. Ordinals are adjectives and agree: la prima volta, il terzo piano, le prime pagine. They are used for floors, kings and popes (Papa Francesco I, Vittorio Emanuele II read as primo, secondo) and centuries (il ventesimo secolo).

rules.title: Telling the time
rules.body: Ask Che ora è? or Che ore sono? Answer with è for one o'clock, noon and midnight, and sono le + number otherwise: È l'una; È mezzogiorno; È mezzanotte; Sono le due; Sono le dieci. Minutes past use e: le tre e dieci, le tre e un quarto, le tre e mezzo (or e mezza). Minutes to use meno: le quattro meno dieci, le quattro meno un quarto. Add di mattina, del pomeriggio, di sera, di notte if needed; timetables use the 24-hour clock (le quindici e trenta). 'At' a time is a + article: all'una, alle otto, a mezzogiorno. A che ora? asks what time.

examples.target: Che ore sono? Sono le tre e un quarto.
examples.en: What time is it? It is a quarter past three.

examples.target: Il treno parte alle otto e venti.

rules.title: Days, months and dates
rules.body: Days: lunedì, martedì, mercoledì, giovedì, venerdì, sabato, domenica. Months: gennaio, febbraio, marzo, aprile, maggio, giugno, luglio, agosto, settembre, ottobre, novembre, dicembre. Both are written in lower case. Dates use il + cardinal number + month, except the first, which is il primo: il tre maggio, il quindici agosto, il primo gennaio. Ask Quanti ne abbiamo oggi? or Che giorno è oggi? Years take nel: nel 2020. A day alone means that one day (lunedì = on Monday); with the article it means every such day (il lunedì = on Mondays). All days are masculine except domenica.

examples.en: Today is the third of May.
On Monday I have an exam.

rules.title: Ages, prices and quantities
rules.body: Age uses avere + anni: Quanti anni hai? Ho trent'anni (the final vowel of venti, trenta etc. is dropped before anni: vent'anni, quarant'anni). Prices: Quanto costa? Quanto costano? Costa dieci euro; euro does not change in the plural, and decimals are read with e: due euro e cinquanta. Quantities use di: un chilo di pane, un litro di latte, un etto (100 g) di prosciutto, una bottiglia di vino. Approximate numbers end in -ina: una decina (about ten), una ventina (about twenty), un centinaio (about a hundred).

examples.en: How old are you? I am twenty.
How much is it? It costs ten euros.

rules.title: tu or Lei
rules.body: tu is for family, friends, children, fellow students and, increasingly, colleagues of the same age; Lei is for strangers, older people, officials, shop and office staff and anyone you would call signore or signora. Lei takes the third-person singular verb and the pronouns La (direct), Le (indirect) and Suo (possessive), often capitalised in writing: Lei è di qui? La ringrazio. Le posso offrire un caffè? Il Suo nome? For more than one person use voi, whether formal or not. Moving to tu is called darsi del tu; an Italian may propose it with Diamoci del tu or Possiamo darci del tu?

examples.en: May I offer you (formal) a coffee?
Shall we use tu with each other?

rules.title: Titles and forms of address
rules.body: The basic titles are signore (Mr, sir), signora (Mrs, Ms, madam) and signorina (Miss, now used mostly for young girls). Before a surname signore drops its -e: signor Rossi, but signora Rossi. Professional titles are used far more than in English: dottore or dottoressa for any graduate and for doctors, professore and professoressa for teachers, avvocato, ingegnere, architetto. Before a name they also drop the final -e: dottor Bianchi, professor Conti, ingegner Rossi. In direct address the title stands alone: Buongiorno, dottore. Scusi, signora.

examples.target: Scusi, signora, è libero questo posto?
examples.en: Excuse me, madam, is this seat free?

rules.title: Greetings and everyday formulas
rules.body: ciao is informal and serves for both hello and goodbye; salve is a neutral hello. buongiorno is used until early afternoon, buonasera after that, buonanotte only when going to bed; arrivederci is the all-purpose goodbye (arrivederLa is the very formal singular). Thanks and replies: grazie, grazie mille, and the answer prego, which also means 'go ahead' and 'you're welcome'. Apologies: scusa (tu), scusi (Lei), mi dispiace (I'm sorry, sympathy). Requests: per favore, per piacere, per cortesia. Meeting: piacere (pleased to meet you), Mi chiamo..., Come ti chiami? / Come si chiama? Polite requests use the conditional: Vorrei un caffè; Potrebbe aiutarmi?

examples.target: Buongiorno! Vorrei un caffè, per favore.
examples.en: Good morning! I'd like a coffee, please.
Excuse me, could you repeat that? (formal)
Pleased to meet you, my name is Anna.

exercises.explain: quattro is four; quattordici is 14 and quaranta is 40.
sette is seven, with a double t.
The ten drops its final vowel before uno: ventuno.
Before otto the final vowel of the ten is dropped: trentotto.

exercises.q: 'ventitré' (23) is written with an accent on the final e.
exercises.explain: tre takes an acute accent at the end of a compound number: ventitré, trentatré.
cento is a hundred and never changes: duecento, trecento.
mille becomes mila in the plural and joins the number: duemila.
Ordinals agree with the noun: il secondo piano.
Hours from two upwards use sono le; only one o'clock, noon and midnight use è.

exercises.q: How do you say 'It is one o'clock'?
exercises.explain: One o'clock is singular: È l'una.

exercises.q: Sono le quattro e ___. (a quarter past four)
exercises.explain: A quarter past is e un quarto: le quattro e un quarto.

exercises.q: What time is 'le cinque meno un quarto'?
exercises.explain: meno un quarto means a quarter to: a quarter to five.

exercises.answer: A che ora parte il treno?
exercises.en: What time does the train leave?

exercises.q: Days of the week and months are written with a capital letter in Italian.
exercises.explain: lunedì, maggio, dicembre are all lower case.

exercises.q: How do you say 'on Monday' (one particular Monday)?
exercises.explain: The bare day means that one day; il lunedì would mean every Monday.

exercises.q: Oggi è il ___ maggio. (the first of May)
exercises.explain: Only the first of the month uses the ordinal: il primo maggio.
Dates other than the first use cardinal numbers: il tre maggio.
Years take nel: nel 1995.

exercises.q: 'euro' does not change in the plural: dieci euro.
exercises.explain: euro is invariable in Italian: un euro, cento euro.

exercises.q: Which is the polite 'you' for one person?
exercises.explain: Lei is the formal singular; voi is for more than one person.

exercises.q: ___ inglese? (Do you speak English? formal, to one person)
exercises.explain: Lei takes the third-person singular verb: Lei parla inglese?

exercises.q: To apologise to a stranger (Lei) you say ___, not scusa.
exercises.explain: scusi is the Lei imperative of scusare; scusa is the tu form.

exercises.q: 'ciao' can be used both for hello and for goodbye among friends.
exercises.explain: ciao is informal and works at both ends of a conversation.

exercises.q: What do you say when introduced to someone?
exercises.explain: Piacere means 'pleased to meet you'; prego answers grazie, salve is a neutral hello.
The standard reply to grazie is prego.
